source_of_truth: This file is the single source of the Prep-3 maths misconception catalogue (FR-4409, decision 22). Edit it here. Never rename a live id: changed wording keeps its id, and a duplicate becomes an alias (FR-1115). Loaded on every deploy by load_misconceptions.py.

misconceptions.label: A chord drawn without both ends on the circle
misconceptions.description: Treats a chord as any line 'across' the circle, including one that stops inside it or runs past it.
misconceptions.signal: At least one endpoint is not on the circle.

refutation.text_md: The direction you drew is fine — a chord does cut across the circle.
What a chord needs is both ENDS on the circle itself. A segment that stops inside, or runs out past the edge, is not one.
It matters because every chord result in this unit — equal chords, distance from the centre, the diameter being longest — is about the two points where it meets the circle.
Put both ends on the circle first, then worry about where it sits.

misconceptions.label: A radius that stops short of the circle
misconceptions.description: Starts correctly at the centre but ends anywhere, as though a radius were a direction rather than a fixed length.
misconceptions.signal: One end is the centre; the other is strictly inside the circle.

refutation.text_md: You started in the right place — the centre — which is the part most people get wrong.
But a radius has to REACH the circle. It is not any segment leaving the centre; it is the fixed distance from the centre to the circle.
That fixed distance is what makes it a circle in the first place: every point on the circle is exactly $r$ from $M$.
So a radius always has two jobs: start at $M$, and end ON the circle.

misconceptions.label: A radius drawn between two points on the circle
misconceptions.description: Builds a segment with both ends on the circle and calls it a radius — the word is attached to 'a line in the circle' rather than to the centre.
misconceptions.signal: Both endpoints satisfy the circle; neither is the centre.

refutation.text_md: Look at what you drew: both ends landed on the circle, and that is a real thing — it is a chord.
A radius is the one segment that always starts at the centre $M$ and stops at the circle. Its whole job is to carry the circle's fixed distance.
That is why every radius of a circle has the same length, and chords do not: a chord can be short or long, but a radius cannot.
Next time, ask where the segment STARTS. Centre to circle is a radius; circle to circle is a chord.

misconceptions.label: A chord drawn without both ends on the circle
misconceptions.description: Treats a chord as any line 'across' the circle, including one that stops inside it or runs past it.
misconceptions.signal: At least one endpoint is not on the circle.

refutation.text_md: The direction you drew is fine — a chord does cut across the circle.
What a chord needs is both ENDS on the circle itself. A segment that stops inside, or runs out past the edge, is not one.
It matters because every chord result in this unit — equal chords, distance from the centre, the diameter being longest — is about the two points where it meets the circle.
Put both ends on the circle first, then worry about where it sits.

misconceptions.label: A diameter taken as any long chord
misconceptions.description: Knows a diameter is long and knows it is a chord, but has not attached the condition that it must pass through the centre.
misconceptions.signal: Both ends on the circle, and the segment misses $M$.

refutation.text_md: What you drew IS a chord — both ends are on the circle, so you have the harder half right.
A diameter is the chord that passes through the centre $M$. Not the longest-looking one: the one through the centre.
Those turn out to be the same thing, and that is the theorem — the diameter is the longest chord precisely BECAUSE it goes through the centre.
Drag one end and watch: the chord grows as it swings towards $M$, and it is longest exactly when it crosses it.

misconceptions.label: Inside and outside reversed
misconceptions.description: Compares the distance from the centre with the radius the wrong way round.
misconceptions.signal: A point with MA > r is called inside, or the reverse.

refutation.text_md: Comparing $MA$ with $r$ is exactly the right test.
Further from the centre than the radius means OUTSIDE: $MA > r$ is outside, $MA < r$ is inside, $MA = r$ is on the circle.
Picture the radius as the wall: past it is outside.

misconceptions.label: A tangent drawn cutting the circle at two points
misconceptions.description: Reads 'tangent' as any line touching or crossing the circle, missing that it meets it exactly once.
misconceptions.signal: The distance from the centre to the line is less than $r$, so the line is a secant.

refutation.text_md: Your line does meet the circle, so you are close — but it meets it TWICE.
A line that cuts a circle at two points is a secant. A tangent touches at exactly one point and then leaves.
The test is a distance: measure from the centre $M$ to the line. Less than $r$ and it cuts twice; equal to $r$ and it touches once; more than $r$ and it misses.
So a tangent is the line whose distance from the centre is exactly the radius.

misconceptions.label: A tangent drawn missing the circle altogether
misconceptions.description: Reads 'tangent' as a line running alongside the circle without meeting it.
misconceptions.signal: The distance from the centre to the line is greater than $r$.

refutation.text_md: Running alongside the circle is the right instinct — a tangent does lie against it.
But it has to TOUCH. Your line stays clear of the circle, so it meets it nowhere at all.
Bring it in until the distance from the centre $M$ equals the radius exactly. That single point of contact is what makes it a tangent.
One number decides it: distance from the centre, compared with $r$.

misconceptions.label: Inscribed angle doubled instead of halved
misconceptions.description: Takes the inscribed angle to equal its arc, or twice it, rather than half.
misconceptions.signal: The answer equals the arc measure or twice it.

refutation.text_md: You have the right pair — the angle and its arc are linked.
The INSCRIBED angle is HALF the arc it subtends; the CENTRAL angle on the same arc is the whole of it.
So a $100^\circ$ arc gives a $50^\circ$ inscribed angle and a $100^\circ$ central angle.
Ask first where the vertex sits: on the circle (inscribed, half) or at the centre (central, whole).

misconceptions.label: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral taken as equal
misconceptions.description: Applies the parallelogram property to a cyclic quadrilateral.
misconceptions.signal: The answer repeats the given angle instead of its supplement.

refutation.text_md: You are using a real property of quadrilaterals — it belongs to parallelograms.
In a CYCLIC quadrilateral the opposite angles are SUPPLEMENTARY: they add to $180^\circ$.
So $m(\angle A) = 100^\circ$ gives $m(\angle C) = 80^\circ$.
Equal opposite angles would only happen when both are $90^\circ$.

misconceptions.label: A touching curve read as having two distinct roots
misconceptions.description: Treats a curve that meets the x-axis at one point as having two different solutions.
misconceptions.signal: The solution set given has two elements where the curve only touches.

refutation.text_md: You are reading roots off the graph, which is exactly what this method is.
Count the points where the curve MEETS the axis: touching at one point means one repeated root, so the solution set has a single element.
Two distinct roots need the curve to cross the axis twice — and that is the case where the discriminant is positive rather than zero.

misconceptions.label: Sign of the discriminant misread
misconceptions.description: Reports real roots when b² − 4ac < 0, or no roots when it is positive.
misconceptions.signal: The stated number of roots contradicts the sign of the discriminant.

refutation.text_md: Computing the discriminant is exactly the right first move.
Its SIGN decides: positive gives two different real roots, zero gives one repeated root, negative gives none in $\mathbb{R}$.
A negative discriminant means the curve never meets the $x$-axis, so the solution set is $\varnothing$.

misconceptions.label: Domain excluded using the numerator
misconceptions.description: Solves the numerator equal to zero when finding which values are excluded.
misconceptions.signal: The excluded value is the zero of the numerator instead of the denominator.

refutation.text_md: You are looking for where something equals zero, which is right.
It is the DENOMINATOR that matters: division by zero is what is undefined.
A zero numerator is perfectly fine — it just makes the whole fraction zero.

misconceptions.label: Only one zero of the denominator excluded
misconceptions.description: Finds one value that breaks the fraction and stops, missing that every factor of the denominator contributes one.
misconceptions.signal: The marked set is a strict subset of the denominator's zeroes.

refutation.text_md: The value you found genuinely does break the fraction — that part is correct.
Every FACTOR of the denominator contributes a forbidden value though, not just the first one.
For $\frac{1}{(x + 2)(x - 3)}$ the denominator is zero when $x = -2$ AND when $x = 3$, so both are excluded.
So the method is: set the whole denominator to zero, solve it completely, and exclude every root you get. The domain is everything else.

misconceptions.label: A compound outcome counted once instead of by its ways
misconceptions.description: Counts 'a total of 7' as one outcome rather than the six ordered pairs that produce it.
misconceptions.signal: $n(E)$ is far smaller than the number of cells in the sample space that satisfy the event.

refutation.text_md: You identified the right event — the totals you picked really do make $7$.
But $n(E)$ counts OUTCOMES, not values. A total of $7$ happens six different ways: $(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)$.
$(1,6)$ and $(6,1)$ are genuinely different outcomes — the first die and the second die did different things — so both are counted.
That is what the grid is for. Every cell is one outcome, so count cells, and $P = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}$.

misconceptions.label: Divided by the wrong total
misconceptions.description: Puts n(S) on top, or divides by the outcomes NOT in A.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is greater than 1, or uses n(S) − n(A) as the denominator.

refutation.text_md: Your two counts are right.
$P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)}$ — favourable outcomes over ALL outcomes, including the favourable ones.
A probability can never exceed $1$; if yours does, the fraction is inverted.

misconceptions.label: Answers zero because the two events sound unrelated
misconceptions.description: Concludes the intersection is empty from the wording of the two events, without listing outcomes to check for a shared one.
misconceptions.signal: Answers $0$ when a shared outcome does exist.

refutation.text_md: Answering $0$ is exactly right when nothing can be in both — so the instinct to check for that is a good one.
The check has to be done on the outcomes, though, not on how the two events sound.
Cards 1 to 10, A even and B prime: 2 is even AND prime, so $A \cap B = \{2\}$ and $P = \frac{1}{10}$, not $0$.
Make it a habit: write out both lists and look for a number in both. Only an empty overlap earns a $0$.

misconceptions.label: Mutually exclusive confused with covering the whole sample space
misconceptions.description: Defines mutually exclusive by the union filling S rather than by the intersection being empty.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses $A \cup B = S$ as the definition of mutually exclusive.

refutation.text_md: You are reaching for a condition on how A and B sit inside S, which is the right kind of answer.
Mutually exclusive means they cannot happen together: $A \cap B = \phi$, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$.
$A \cup B = S$ says something else — that between them they cover every outcome. Two events can do that and still overlap.
Rolling a die: 'greater than 2' and 'less than 5' cover everything between them, yet 3 and 4 are in both. Covering is not the same as excluding.

misconceptions.label: Reports the probability of one event instead of the intersection
misconceptions.description: Computes P(A) correctly and stops, without intersecting with B.
misconceptions.signal: The answer equals P(A) or P(B) rather than P(A ∩ B).

refutation.text_md: Your value for the single event is right, so the counting is not the problem.
The question asks for A and B TOGETHER, which needs the outcomes shared by both.
A die, A even and B odd: no number is both, so $A \cap B = \phi$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0$ — even though $P(A) = \frac{1}{2}$.
Before answering, read the last line again and ask which event it names: A, B, or both at once.

misconceptions.label: A and B read as 'A happens and B does not'
misconceptions.description: Reads the intersection as one event occurring in place of the other rather than alongside it.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses 'the occurrence of A only'.

refutation.text_md: You are right that $A \cap B$ is stricter than 'either one' — it does narrow things down.
But it narrows to outcomes where A and B happen TOGETHER, not to A by itself.
'A only' is the part of A outside B, which is a different region of the Venn diagram and has its own notation.
Check yourself with one outcome: if it is in both lists, it belongs to $A \cap B$.

misconceptions.label: A and B read as 'at least one of them' instead of 'both'
misconceptions.description: Treats the intersection as the union: takes any outcome in either event rather than only the shared ones.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses 'at least one of the two events', or computes a probability matching the union.

refutation.text_md: You have the right idea that two events are being combined — that is what the question is about.
$A \cap B$ is the event that BOTH happen at the same time. 'At least one of them' is $A \cup B$, the union.
The symbols are worth separating once: $\cap$ is the overlap in the Venn diagram — the part inside both circles — and $\cup$ is everything inside either circle.
A phrase to keep: $\cap$ means AND, $\cup$ means OR.

maps.choice_text: the occurrence of at least one of the two events

misconceptions.label: Counts 'together' by adding the two event sizes
misconceptions.description: Adds n(A) and n(B) instead of counting the outcomes common to both.
misconceptions.signal: The numerator equals n(A) + n(B).

refutation.text_md: You counted both events correctly — that part is done.
Adding them answers a different question. For 'A and B together' you want only the outcomes appearing in BOTH lists.
Cards 1 to 12, A divisible by 3 is $\{3, 6, 9, 12\}$ and B divisible by 4 is $\{4, 8, 12\}$. Only $12$ is in both, so $n(A \cap B) = 1$ and $P = \frac{1}{12}$.
Adding the sizes is a move for the union, and even there it double-counts the overlap.

misconceptions.label: Overlap counted twice in a union
misconceptions.description: Adds P(A) and P(B) without subtracting P(A ∩ B).
misconceptions.signal: The answer exceeds the correct union probability by exactly P(A ∩ B).

refutation.text_md: Adding the two is the right starting point.
Outcomes in BOTH events get counted once in each, so they are counted twice. Subtract the overlap: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
When the events are mutually exclusive the overlap is empty and the subtraction changes nothing — which is why the simple sum sometimes appears to work.

misconceptions.label: Complement not subtracted from 1
misconceptions.description: Reports P(A) itself, or inverts it, instead of 1 − P(A).
misconceptions.signal: The answer and P(A) do not sum to 1.

refutation.text_md: You have the right probability in hand.
An event and its complement cover everything that can happen, so they sum to $1$: $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$.
Quick check: add your two probabilities. If they do not make $1$, one of them is not the complement.

misconceptions.label: Antecedent and consequent exchanged
misconceptions.description: Names the second term of a ratio as the antecedent.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the consequent, or the ratio written in reverse order.

refutation.text_md: You have identified a term of the ratio correctly.
In $4 : 9$ the FIRST term, $4$, is the antecedent and the second, $9$, is the consequent.
The order matters: $4 : 9$ and $9 : 4$ are different ratios.

misconceptions.label: Equivalent ratios found by adding rather than multiplying
misconceptions.description: Looks for a constant difference between terms instead of a constant multiplier.
misconceptions.signal: The chosen ratio keeps the gap between the terms, not their quotient.

refutation.text_md: You spotted a pattern — but it is the wrong one for ratios.
Equivalent ratios come from MULTIPLYING both terms by the same number: $3 : 5$ times $4$ gives $12 : 20$.
$5 : 7$ keeps the difference of $2$, which does not preserve the ratio: $\frac{3}{5} \neq \frac{5}{7}$.

misconceptions.label: Only one term multiplied
misconceptions.description: Scales the terms of a ratio by different factors.
misconceptions.signal: One term is scaled and the other is not, or each by a different amount.

refutation.text_md: Multiplying to find an equivalent ratio is the right move.
Both terms must be multiplied by the SAME number. $9 : 25$ comes from $3 \times 3$ and $5 \times 5$ — different factors, so a different ratio.
$3 : 5$ times $4$ gives $12 : 20$; check by simplifying back.

misconceptions.label: A ratio read as fixing the actual values
misconceptions.description: Takes a/b = 2/7 to mean a = 2 and b = 7 exactly, rather than a = 2m, b = 7m.
misconceptions.signal: The answer asserts specific values, or a specific sum, from a ratio alone.

refutation.text_md: Those values do satisfy the ratio — they are one possible pair.
But a ratio fixes only the RELATIONSHIP: $a = 2m$ and $b = 7m$ for some $m \neq 0$. $a = 4, b = 14$ works just as well.
That is also why $a + b = 9$ is not certain: the sum is $9m$, which depends on $m$.

misconceptions.label: Ratio not reduced to simplest form
misconceptions.description: Gives the raw ratio where the simplest form is asked.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is a correct but unreduced equivalent.

refutation.text_md: The comparison you wrote is correct — it is the same ratio.
Simplest form means dividing both terms by their highest common factor: $6 : 8$ has HCF $2$, giving $3 : 4$.
Check afterwards that the two terms share no factor other than $1$.

misconceptions.label: Terms of a ratio added together
misconceptions.description: Combines the two terms into their sum rather than keeping the comparison.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is a single number equal to the sum of the terms.

refutation.text_md: Both numbers are the right ones.
A ratio COMPARES two quantities; it is not a single total. $4 : 9$ stays as a pair.
$13$ would be the total number of parts, which is a different (and sometimes useful) quantity.

misconceptions.label: Adding the same number to both terms assumed to preserve the ratio
misconceptions.description: Carries the rule for multiplication over to addition.
misconceptions.signal: The student asserts the ratio is unchanged after adding to both terms.

refutation.text_md: The rule you are thinking of is real — but it is about multiplying.
Multiplying both terms by the same nonzero number leaves a ratio unchanged. ADDING does not: $3 : 5$ becomes $4 : 6 = 2 : 3$, which is different.
Test it with the numbers whenever you are unsure — one example settles it.

misconceptions.label: Means and extremes exchanged
misconceptions.description: Names b and c as the extremes of a/b = c/d.
misconceptions.signal: The answer gives the middle pair where the outer pair is asked.

refutation.text_md: You have the right pair of terms in mind, just the other pair.
Written as $a : b = c : d$, the EXTREMES are the outer terms $a$ and $d$; the means are the inner terms $b$ and $c$.
The rule 'product of the extremes = product of the means' is exactly $ad = bc$.

misconceptions.label: Proportion defined as a sum or product of ratios
misconceptions.description: Treats a proportion as an operation between ratios rather than an equality of them.
misconceptions.signal: The definition chosen involves adding or multiplying two ratios.

refutation.text_md: You know a proportion involves two ratios.
It is their EQUALITY: $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$. Nothing is added or multiplied — the statement is that the two comparisons are the same.
That equality is what lets you cross-multiply.

misconceptions.label: Cross-multiplication paired incorrectly
misconceptions.description: Multiplies numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator, or top-to-bottom on the same side.
misconceptions.signal: The stated product is ab = cd or ac = bd rather than ad = bc.

refutation.text_md: Cross-multiplying is the right tool here.
It pairs each numerator with the OTHER fraction's denominator: $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$ gives $a \times d = b \times c$.
Draw the two diagonals of the equality and multiply along each one — they cross, which is where the name comes from.

misconceptions.label: A direct relationship solved by matching products
misconceptions.description: Applies the inverse rule to a straightforwardly proportional situation.
misconceptions.signal: The answer equals $\frac{ab}{c}$ where $\frac{bc}{a}$ was required.

refutation.text_md: You have the inverse rule solid, which is the one most people forget.
This relationship goes the other way though: as one quantity grows, so does the other.
When both rise together the two RATIOS stay equal — $3 : 4 = 9 : 12$, because $3 \div 4$ and $9 \div 12$ are the same number.
One question sorts it every time: when this goes up, does that go up or down?

misconceptions.label: An inverse relationship solved by matching ratios
misconceptions.description: Applies the direct-variation move — set the two quotients equal and cross-multiply — to a situation where one quantity falls as the other rises.
misconceptions.signal: The answer equals $\frac{bc}{a}$ where $\frac{ab}{c}$ was required.

refutation.text_md: Cross-multiplying is a good, reliable move — it is just the wrong one here.
In DIRECT variation the two quotients match: more of one, proportionally more of the other.
In INVERSE variation the two PRODUCTS match: $6$ workers $\times 10$ days $= 60$, so $4$ workers need $60 \div 4 = 15$ days.
Before reaching for either, ask the sentence out loud: if one goes up and the other goes DOWN, it is the product that stays fixed.

misconceptions.label: Primary resources assumed to be the quick and cheap option
misconceptions.description: Reverses the trade-off: field data is accurate but costly; secondary data is cheap but second-hand.
misconceptions.signal: The answer attributes low cost or speed to primary collection.

refutation.text_md: There is a real trade-off here, and you are reaching for it.
It runs the other way: PRIMARY resources are the accurate ones and cost the most time, effort and money. SECONDARY resources save all three but you did not control how they were gathered.
Accuracy costs; convenience costs accuracy.

maps.choice_text: They are the most accurate of all resources

misconceptions.label: Ready-made data called a primary resource
misconceptions.description: Classifies data taken from published records as field data because the student gathered it themselves.
misconceptions.signal: A record, website or publication is described as a primary resource.

refutation.text_md: Collecting the data yourself does feel like field work — that is the honest confusion here.
What decides it is where the data ORIGINATED. Figures already compiled by someone else are SECONDARY, however you obtained them.
Primary means you generated the observations: a questionnaire you distributed, an interview you conducted, a count you made.

maps.choice_text: Hany, who copied population figures from a newspaper report
Omar, who downloaded last year's exam statistics from the ministry website
Sara, who used tables published by a statistics agency

misconceptions.label: A sample assumed to be more accurate than a census
misconceptions.description: Justifies sampling by accuracy rather than by cost, size or destructive testing.
misconceptions.signal: The reason given for sampling is that it is more accurate.

refutation.text_md: Sampling is the right method in that situation — the reason is what slipped.
A census covers every value, so it is the MORE accurate method. We sample when a census is impossible or self-defeating: the society is gigantic, or the test destroys what it measures.
Testing every lamp until it burns out would leave nothing to sell.

maps.choice_text: Because samples always give more accurate outcomes than a census

misconceptions.label: The middle value offered where the average was asked for
misconceptions.description: Builds or picks a set whose MIDDLE value is the target, having read 'mean' as 'the one in the middle'.
misconceptions.signal: The set's median equals the target while its mean does not.

refutation.text_md: Your middle value is exactly right — so you found the median, and that is a real statistic.
The mean is a different idea: it is the total shared out equally. Add every value, divide by how many there are.
They come apart the moment the data is lopsided. In $1, 2, 6, 9, 10$ the median is $6$ but the mean is $5.6$ — one small value drags the average down and leaves the middle untouched.
A quick check for the mean: for $n$ values to average $m$, the TOTAL has to be $m \times n$. Add yours up and see.

misconceptions.label: The average offered where the middle value was asked for
misconceptions.description: Builds a set with the target mean when the median was asked for.
misconceptions.signal: The set's mean equals the target while its median does not.

refutation.text_md: The arithmetic is right — you built a set that averages to the target.
The median is not an average, though. Put the values in ORDER and take the one in the middle.
That ordering step is the whole difference. The mean feels every value; the median only cares about position, which is why one huge value moves the mean and leaves the median where it was.
With an even count there is no single middle, so the median is the mean of the two middle values.

misconceptions.label: A mode assumed to exist in every set
misconceptions.description: Offers some value as 'the mode' for a set where nothing repeats, or where several values tie.
misconceptions.signal: No value repeats, or two or more tie for the highest frequency.

refutation.text_md: Looking for the most frequent value is exactly the right move.
But a set does not have to have one. If every value appears once, there is no mode at all — 'none' is the correct answer, not a failure to find it.
And if two values tie for the most frequent, the set has TWO modes. Both get reported.
So the mode is the only one of the three averages that can be missing or doubled. That is worth remembering when a question seems to have no answer.

misconceptions.label: Range confused with the mean
misconceptions.description: Averages the values instead of subtracting the smallest from the largest.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the mean of the set.

refutation.text_md: The mean is a real and useful number — it just answers a different question.
The mean says where the values SIT; the range says how far apart they are.
Range $=$ greatest $-$ smallest. Nothing is divided.

misconceptions.label: The range assumed to reflect every value
misconceptions.description: Misses that the range depends only on the two extremes, which is precisely its weakness.
misconceptions.signal: The stated weakness of the range involves the mean, the count or the middle value.

refutation.text_md: You are right that the range has a weakness — this is the one.
It uses ONLY the greatest and smallest values. Everything in between could move anywhere without changing it.
That is why the standard deviation exists: it is affected by every value in the set.

maps.choice_text: the middle value of the set

misconceptions.label: Zero dispersion read as zero values
misconceptions.description: Takes 'dispersion = 0' to mean the values or the mean are zero, rather than that the values are identical.
misconceptions.signal: The answer claims a value, mean or count of zero.

refutation.text_md: Zero is doing something specific here, and it is worth being exact about what.
Dispersion measures how far apart the values are. Zero dispersion means they are ALL EQUAL — not that they are zero.
$7, 7, 7, 7$ has dispersion zero and a mean of $7$.

misconceptions.label: Squared deviations summed but not averaged
misconceptions.description: Divides by nothing before taking the root, so the sum is used in place of its mean.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is √(Σd²) rather than √(Σd²/n).

refutation.text_md: Your deviations and their squares are right.
They have to be AVERAGED before the root: divide the sum by $n$, the number of values.
Sum $= 8$, $n = 4$, so the average is $2$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{2}$ — not $\sqrt{8}$.
The formula carries the division inside the root: $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$.

misconceptions.label: Dividing by n − 1 instead of n
misconceptions.description: Uses the sample standard deviation formula, which this curriculum does not define. Usually arrives from outside the book — a tutor, an older sibling, a calculator mode, or an AI assistant.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is larger than the expected one by the factor √(n/(n−1)); for five values, 2.24 where 2.00 is expected.

refutation.text_md: Good question, and you have not made a mistake in the arithmetic — you have met a second formula that exists in statistics.

Your book defines the standard deviation of a SET OF VALUES as $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$ — divide by $n$, the number of values. That is the one to use here, and the one your exam will mark.

The version with $n - 1$ belongs to a different situation: when the values are a SAMPLE and you want to estimate the spread of a much larger group you did not measure. Dividing by $n - 1$ makes that estimate slightly larger, because a small sample tends to look tighter than the group it came from.
Your syllabus does not cover that case, so: divide by $n$. If a calculator or a website gives you a different number, check whether it used the sample setting.

misconceptions.label: Standard deviation confused with the range or the mean
misconceptions.description: Defines σ as a spread already named, or as the average of the values themselves.
misconceptions.signal: The definition chosen is the range, or the mean, rather than the root of the mean squared deviation.

refutation.text_md: Those are all real statistics — they just answer different questions.
$\sigma$ is the positive square root of the AVERAGE OF THE SQUARES OF THE DEVIATIONS from the mean.
The mean says where the values sit; the range and $\sigma$ say how spread out they are, and $\sigma$ uses every value while the range uses two.

maps.choice_text: the sum of the values divided by their range
the difference between the greatest and smallest values

misconceptions.label: Square root never taken
misconceptions.description: Stops at the variance and reports it as the standard deviation.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the square of the correct standard deviation.

refutation.text_md: Every step up to there was right — you found the average of the squared deviations correctly.
That average is the VARIANCE. The standard deviation is its positive square root.
For $3, 5, 5, 7$: mean $5$, squared deviations $4, 0, 0, 4$, average $2$, so $\sigma = \sqrt{2}$.
One last step, every time: take the root.

misconceptions.label: Frequency substituted for the value
misconceptions.description: Puts k where x belongs in the frequency-distribution formula.
misconceptions.signal: Deviations are computed from the frequencies rather than from the values.

refutation.text_md: You are using the right formula — the letters are what got crossed.
$x$ is the VALUE (for classes, the centre of the set); $k$ is how many times it occurs.
The deviation $(x - \bar{x})$ measures how far a value sits from the mean; a frequency has no distance from the mean.

misconceptions.label: Degree divided into 100 parts
misconceptions.description: Applies decimal place-value to degrees and minutes, so 0.25° is read as 25'.
misconceptions.signal: The minutes in the answer are the decimal digits of the degrees.

refutation.text_md: Decimals usually do work that way — angles are the exception.
A degree is divided into $60$ minutes, and a minute into $60$ seconds. So $0.25^\circ = 0.25 \times 60 = 15'$, giving $20^\circ\ 15'$.
Multiply the decimal part by $60$; never copy the digits across.

misconceptions.label: Minutes and seconds confused
misconceptions.description: Names 60 seconds as the subdivision of a degree, or leaves a decimal inside the minutes.
misconceptions.signal: The unit named for the first subdivision of a degree is the second.

refutation.text_md: The number $60$ is right — it is the unit that slipped.
A degree splits into $60$ MINUTES; each minute then splits into $60$ SECONDS.
So a leftover decimal in the minutes is converted again: $0.6' = 0.6 \times 60 = 36''$.

misconceptions.label: Opposite and adjacent sides exchanged
misconceptions.description: Takes the side next to the angle where the side facing it is required, swapping sine with cosine or inverting the tangent.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the ratio of the other acute angle, or the reciprocal.

refutation.text_md: You picked the right two sides — the question is which is which.
'Opposite' means the side FACING the angle, across the triangle from it; 'adjacent' is the side touching it that is not the hypotenuse.
Mark the angle you are working from first, then label the three sides relative to THAT angle. They change when you switch angles.
$\sin = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, $\cos = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, $\tan = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$.

misconceptions.label: Ratio written upside down
misconceptions.description: Divides the hypotenuse by a leg instead of the leg by the hypotenuse.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is greater than 1 for a sine or cosine, which is impossible.

refutation.text_md: The two sides are correct — they are the wrong way up.
$\sin$ and $\cos$ put the HYPOTENUSE on the bottom, so both are always less than $1$ in a right-angled triangle.
An answer above $1$ for a sine or cosine is a signal to flip the fraction and check.

misconceptions.label: Hypotenuse used in the tangent
misconceptions.description: Builds tan from a leg and the hypotenuse rather than from the two legs.
misconceptions.signal: The tangent is reported as a sine or cosine value.

refutation.text_md: You are choosing between the three sides, which is the right process.
The tangent is the only ratio that does NOT use the hypotenuse: opposite over adjacent, the two legs.
If the hypotenuse appears in your fraction, you have written a sine or a cosine.

misconceptions.label: Opposite and adjacent exchanged when computing a ratio
misconceptions.description: Labels the sides relative to the wrong acute angle, or swaps opposite with adjacent.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the ratio of the other acute angle, or the reciprocal.

refutation.text_md: You chose the right two sides — which is which is the question.
Label the sides relative to the angle you are ASKED about: 'opposite' faces it across the triangle, 'adjacent' touches it and is not the hypotenuse.
Both labels swap when you move to the other acute angle, which is why $\sin A = \cos C$ in a right-angled triangle.
Mark the angle first, then label, then choose the ratio.

misconceptions.label: Coordinates added instead of subtracted
misconceptions.description: Uses x1 + x2 where x2 − x1 is required, so the distance comes out as a sum.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the sum of the coordinates rather than their difference.

refutation.text_md: You are combining the coordinates, which is the right idea.
Distance measures a DIFFERENCE: $AB = |x_2 - x_1|$ along the $x$-axis, so $|6 - 2| = 4$.
$8$ is $6 + 2$. Adding gives you a bigger number that no longer describes a gap.

misconceptions.label: Differences added before squaring
misconceptions.description: Computes (dx + dy) rather than √(dx² + dy²).
misconceptions.signal: The answer equals the sum of the two coordinate differences.

refutation.text_md: Both differences are right — it is how they combine that changes.
They cannot simply be added: the two directions are perpendicular, so Pythagoras applies. $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10$, not $6 + 8 = 14$.
Square, add, then root — in that order.

misconceptions.label: Distance read from one point only
misconceptions.description: Reports one point's coordinate as the distance instead of the separation between both.
misconceptions.signal: The answer equals one of the given coordinates.

refutation.text_md: That number is in the question, which is why it is tempting.
A distance always involves BOTH points: $|6 - 2| = 4$, not $6$ or $2$ on their own.
Ask what the number is measuring FROM as well as to.

misconceptions.label: Square root never taken in the distance rule
misconceptions.description: Stops at the sum of the squares.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the square of the correct distance.

refutation.text_md: Your squares are right: $6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100$.
That $100$ is the square of the distance. The rule ends with a root: $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
$AB = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$ — the root is part of the formula, not an optional tidy-up.

misconceptions.label: Three collinear points treated as a triangle
misconceptions.description: Misses that AB + BC = AC means the points lie on one line and enclose no area.
misconceptions.signal: The answer describes a triangle although the three distances satisfy AB + BC = AC.

refutation.text_md: Your three lengths are right, and you are reading them against each other, which is the method.
When the two shorter distances ADD EXACTLY to the longest, the points cannot form a triangle — the 'path' $A \to B \to C$ is as short as going straight, so $B$ lies on $\overline{AC}$.
They are collinear. A genuine triangle needs $AB + BC > AC$.

misconceptions.label: Right angle placed at the wrong vertex
misconceptions.description: Identifies that the triangle is right-angled but names a vertex other than the one where the two shorter sides meet.
misconceptions.signal: The named vertex is not the one opposite the longest side.

refutation.text_md: You correctly spotted that it IS right-angled.
The right angle sits at the vertex OPPOSITE the longest side — where the two shorter sides meet.
Compute all three lengths, find the largest, and the right angle is at the vertex not touching it.

misconceptions.label: Midpoint built from differences or sums without halving
misconceptions.description: Subtracts or adds the coordinates instead of averaging them.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the sum of the coordinates, or their difference halved.

refutation.text_md: You are working with both points, which is right.
The midpoint AVERAGES: $M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2},\ \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$, so $\left(\frac{2+4}{2},\ \frac{6+0}{2}\right) = (3, 3)$.
$(6, 6)$ is the sum with the halving forgotten. A midpoint must land BETWEEN the two points — check that it does.

misconceptions.label: Run divided by rise
misconceptions.description: Computes Δx/Δy instead of Δy/Δx.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the reciprocal of the correct slope.

refutation.text_md: Both differences are right — the fraction is upside down.
Slope is RISE over RUN: $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$.
A memory hook: slope answers 'how much does it climb for each step sideways', so the climb is on top.

misconceptions.label: The sign of the slope lost
misconceptions.description: Gets the steepness right but the direction wrong, usually by subtracting the coordinates in opposite orders top and bottom.
misconceptions.signal: The drawn line's gradient is the negative of the required one.

refutation.text_md: The size of your slope is right, so the arithmetic is fine — it is the direction that slipped.
Subtract in the SAME order top and bottom: $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$. Reversing one of them and not the other flips the sign.
Then check it against the picture: a line going up to the right has a positive slope, and down to the right is negative.
The picture is the fastest check you have. Glance at the line and ask which way it leans before you trust the number.

misconceptions.label: Sign flipped without taking the reciprocal
misconceptions.description: Uses −m for a perpendicular slope instead of −1/m.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the negative of the original slope.

refutation.text_md: Changing the sign is half of the rule, and you got that half.
Perpendicular slopes multiply to $-1$, so the other slope is $\frac{-1}{m}$ — flip the fraction AND change the sign.
Check by multiplying: if the product is not $-1$, the lines are not perpendicular.

misconceptions.label: No meeting point read as "every x is a solution"
misconceptions.description: When the curve does not meet the x-axis, concludes that every real number solves the equation, instead of none.
misconceptions.signal: The solution set given is $\mathbb{R}$ although the curve does not meet the $x$-axis.

refutation.text_md: A root is a value of $x$ that makes $f(x) = 0$. On the graph it is a point where the curve sits exactly on the $x$-axis.
If the curve never meets the $x$-axis, no such point exists: no value of $x$ makes $f(x) = 0$.
So the solution set is empty, $\varnothing$. $\mathbb{R}$ would mean that every $x$ works, which is the opposite.

misconceptions.label: Roots read off the numbers in the equation
misconceptions.description: Takes numbers written in the equation (its coefficients) as its roots, instead of reading where the curve meets the x-axis.
misconceptions.signal: The solution set is made of numbers taken from the equation itself.

refutation.text_md: The numbers written in the equation, its coefficients, describe the curve. They are not its roots.
A root is an $x$ that makes $f(x) = 0$: on the graph, the $x$-coordinate of a point where the curve meets the $x$-axis. Substituting a candidate tells you at once whether it is one.
Read the roots from the meeting points: two, one, or none. When the curve does not meet the axis, the solution set is $\varnothing$.

misconceptions.label: Treating an ordered pair like a set, so order does not matter
misconceptions.description: The student thinks (a, b) and (b, a) are the same, as if the pair were just the set {a, b} with no order.
misconceptions.signal: Says (3, 5) equals (5, 3), or matches the numbers in the wrong positions when finding unknowns.

refutation.text_md: You are noticing that (3, 5) and (5, 3) use the same two numbers, which is true. But in an ordered pair the position of each number matters, so the same numbers are not enough.
A set like $\{3, 5\}$ has no order, so $\{3, 5\} = \{5, 3\}$. An ordered pair is different: the first number is how far along the x-axis, and the second is how far up.

Plot both. For (3, 5) go 3 along and 5 up. For (5, 3) go 5 along and 3 up. These land in different places, and each ordered pair is one and only one point. Different points mean different pairs, so $(3, 5) \neq (5, 3)$.
The same idea is why you match first with first and second with second. In $(x - 2, 3) = (5, y + 1)$, the first numbers give $x - 2 = 5$ and the second numbers give $3 = y + 1$.
When you compare two ordered pairs, check position by position: first with first, second with second. If $a \neq b$, then $(a, b) \neq (b, a)$.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is supported by the book's remarks (a≠b gives (a,b)≠(b,a), and (a,b) is not the set {a,b}). The refutation matches the canonical plotting argument for (3,5) vs (5,3) and the first-with-first, second-with-second matching in Example 1. It makes no wrong claims and cites no question ids, pages or review history. It rebuts the set-like thinking directly instead of only restating the method.

misconceptions.label: Treats X×Y and Y×X as the same set
misconceptions.description: The student assumes that swapping the two sets gives the same set of pairs, as if the order of the sets did not matter.
misconceptions.signal: States X×Y = Y×X, or writes the same pairs for both products, or answers 'they are equal' when asked to compare them.

refutation.text_md: You may be thinking that, since the same elements are being paired, the two products must be the same set. You are right about one thing: the two products do have the same number of elements. But the sets themselves are different.
In $X\times Y$ the first element of every pair comes from $X$ and the second from $Y$. Take $X=\{a, b\}$ and $Y=\{-1, 0, 3\}$. Then $X\times Y$ contains $(a, -1)$.

In $Y\times X$ the first element comes from $Y$ and the second from $X$, so it contains $(-1, a)$ instead. The pair $(a, -1)$ is not the same as $(-1, a)$, because the order inside an ordered pair matters. So $X\times Y\neq Y\times X$.

What does match is the count: $n(X\times Y)=n(X)\times n(Y)$ and $n(Y\times X)=n(Y)\times n(X)$, and multiplication does not depend on order. Both have $2\times 3=6$ elements, yet the pairs are different. The two products are equal only when $X=Y$, because then both are $X^2$.
To compare, write out both lists of pairs. For $X\times Y$ put the element from $X$ first. For $Y\times X$ put the element from $Y$ first. Then check whether the pairs are really the same.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and backed by the book's remark that X×Y ≠ Y×X when X ≠ Y. The refutation is correct and matches the book's examples. It uses the book's example sets and the book's count rule n(X×Y)=n(X)×n(Y), and it notes that the products are equal only when X=Y. It speaks to this error and does not just restate the method. It cites no question ids, pages or figures.

misconceptions.label: Adds the sizes to count the pairs in X×X
misconceptions.description: The student expects X×X to have $n(X)+n(X)$ pairs, for example 6 pairs for a 3-element set, and so draws too few arrows or points.
misconceptions.signal: States that $n(X\times X)=6$ for a 3-element set.

refutation.text_md: You combined the sizes by adding, $3+3=6$. Each set does have 3 elements, but a Cartesian product pairs elements up. It does not join the two sets together.

Each of the 3 choices for the first projection goes with each of the 3 choices for the second. For $X=\{3, 4, 8\}$ this gives $(3, 3), (3, 4), (3, 8)$, then $(4, 3), (4, 4), (4, 8)$, then $(8, 3), (8, 4), (8, 8)$. That is 9 pairs, not 6.
So $n(X\times X)=3\times 3=9$. In the Cartesian diagram, this is 9 intersection points.
Before drawing, multiply the sizes to know how many arrows or points to expect, then check your diagram against that number.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real (adding gives 6, not 9). The refutation lists all 9 pairs and gives n(X×X)=3×3=9, consistent with the book's rule and example. It argues against the addition error specifically. The signal matches the error and would not misdiagnose a student.

misconceptions.label: Leaves out the arrows for pairs with equal projections
misconceptions.description: When drawing X×X, the student draws arrows only between different elements and skips pairs like (3, 3), because an arrow 'must go somewhere else'.

refutation.text_md: You drew arrows between different elements and left out pairs such as $(3, 3)$. Those arrows between different points are right. The pairs whose two parts match are the ones that went missing.
$(3, 3)$ is an ordered pair in $X\times X$ just as $(3, 4)$ is. Each ordered pair needs its own arrow, starting at its first projection and ending at its second projection.
For $X=\{3, 4, 8\}$ the product has 9 pairs. If you skip $(3, 3)$, $(4, 4)$ and $(8, 8)$, you draw only 6 arrows, so the diagram shows 6 pairs instead of all 9.

When the first projection equals the second, the arrow starts and ends at the same point. Draw it as a buttonhole on that point. Then count your arrows: there should be one for every pair in your list.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and supported by the book's remark on buttonhole arrows for equal-projection pairs. The refutation is correct: 9 pairs, 6 arrows if the 3 equal pairs are skipped. It matches the canonical buttonhole method and argues against this specific error. It cites no outside references.

misconceptions.label: Writes the pairs from Y to X instead of from X to Y
misconceptions.description: The student writes each ordered pair with the book type first and the student second, or draws the arrows from the books back to the students.
misconceptions.signal: Pairs such as (science, a) or (history, b), where the first entry comes from Y instead of X.

refutation.text_md: You have the right connections: $a$ and science really do go together. The slip is in which way round you wrote them.
A relation from $X$ to $Y$ starts in $X$ and ends in $Y$. Here $X$ is the students $\{a, b, c, d, e\}$ and $Y$ is the types of books $\{\text{science, literature, culture, history}\}$.

In the arrow diagram the arrow begins at the student and ends at the type of book he reads. An ordered pair follows the same direction: the first entry is where the arrow starts, the second is where it ends.
Student $a$ read science, so the pair is $(a, \text{science})$, not $(\text{science}, a)$. Student $b$ read history, so the pair is $(b, \text{history})$.

For each pair, ask: which element is the student? Put that first, then the book type. This gives $R = \{(a, \text{science}), (a, \text{culture}), (b, \text{history}), (c, \text{literature}), (e, \text{history})\}$.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and the book's remark supports it: arrows run from the student (X) to the book type (Y), so pairs are (student, book). The refutation uses the same sets and the same direction. Its examples (a, science) and (b, history) are correct, and its final R matches the canonical R exactly. It addresses the reversal itself and cites no outside figure, page or review history.

covers.text: Built Y×X — the pairs are the right numbers in the wrong order

misconceptions.label: Draws every linear function's line through (0, 0)
misconceptions.description: The student carries the 'straight line through the origin' idea over to functions like f(x)=ax+b with b≠0 and draws the line through (0, 0) instead of plotting the ordered pairs from a table.
misconceptions.signal: The line for a function such as f(x)=2x-3 is drawn through (0, 0), or (0, 0) is listed as one of the table's ordered pairs.

refutation.text_md: You remembered that a line like $f(x)=ax$ passes through the origin $(0, 0)$. That is true, but only for that form, where there is no number added or subtracted.
For $f(x)=2x-3$ the line is not of that form, so test it: $f(0)=2(0)-3=-3$. When $x=0$ the output is $-3$, not $0$, so $(0, 0)$ is not on the graph.
The other pairs in the table are $f(1)=2-3=-1$ and $f(2)=4-3=1$. The points $(0, -3)$, $(1, -1)$, $(2, 1)$ lie on a straight line that crosses the vertical axis at $-3$.
Next time, substitute two or three values of $x$ into the rule, write the ordered pairs in a table, plot them, and draw the straight line through them. Do not assume it goes through $(0, 0)$.

provenance.verifier_reason: Over-generalising the book's y=ax-through-origin rule to f(x)=ax+b is a real, evidence-backed error. The refutation's arithmetic matches the canonical solution (f(0)=-3, f(1)=-1, f(2)=1). It tests (0,0) directly and uses the book's table-and-plot method. It cites no outside references, and 'crosses the vertical axis at -3' is only a plain description of the plotted point (0,-3).
